## {.quote-slide .no-title}

::: {.quote-text}
"The take-home essay was already a weak signal. Now it is a test of whose AI wrote the better answer. The question is not how to stop students using AI --- it is [what we should be measuring instead.]{.amber}"
:::

::: {.quote-source}
The problem every assessment in your course now faces
:::

## The Problem, Stated Plainly

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-red}
[What broke]{.card-title}

- AI drafts the essay, the memo, the code, the problem set
- Take-home work no longer tells you what the student can do
- Detection is unreliable --- and biased against non-native writers
:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[The move]{.card-title}

- Stop trying to keep AI out of everything
- Decide, per assessment, where AI belongs and where it cannot reach
- Measure [judgment]{.accent} --- the thing AI does not supply
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Four responses this session: flip the classroom, assign software that has to run, make students check AI, and hold secure exams that AI cannot fake.
:::

## Two Lanes {.section-divider}

## Put Security Where It Can Be Enforced

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Secure lane]{.card-title}

- Supervised, in-person --- exams, orals, in-class work
- No devices, or locked-down ones
- Assessment *of* learning: this is where the grade's integrity lives
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Open lane]{.card-title}

- Take-home, AI-allowed and scaffolded
- Students use every tool they will use at work
- Assessment *for* learning: practice, feedback, building
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The mistake is pretending the open lane can be secured. Let it be AI-rich; concentrate integrity in the lane you can actually control.
:::

## Flipped Classroom {.section-divider}

## Move Content Out, Judgment In

::: {.step-flow}
::: {.step-card}
::: {.step-icon}
🎧
:::
::: {.step-title}
Tutorbot
:::
::: {.step-desc}
Student absorbs the concept before class, asking questions as they go
:::
:::
::: {.step-card}
::: {.step-icon}
📋
:::
::: {.step-title}
Case
:::
::: {.step-desc}
A case built on that concept; student prepares a recommendation
:::
:::
::: {.step-card}
::: {.step-icon}
🎙️
:::
::: {.step-title}
Cold call
:::
::: {.step-desc}
Class time tests understanding through discussion
:::
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The flipped classroom is an assessment strategy: the graded moment moves into the room, where it is supervised, and rides on discussion rather than a document a bot could have written.
:::

## What the Logs Tell You

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Before class]{.card-title}

- The tutorbot's question log shows what confused people, at 9 p.m., before class
- Pre-case writeups surface who caught the hook
- You walk in knowing where to aim
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[In class]{.card-title}

- A cold-call bank keyed to case details, grouped by concept
- Each question notes the answer to listen for
- Starred questions separate who understood from who skimmed
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Formative signal you never had before --- and it is generated alongside the case, not hand-built.
:::

## Software Deliverables {.section-divider}

## Assign Things That Have to Run

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Why it resists faking]{.card-title}

- A model, an app, or an agent either works or it doesn't
- The grade is on a deliverable you can *execute*, not prose you have to trust
- Using AI to build it is the point, not the cheat
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[What you can see]{.card-title}

- The commit history: who built what, when, in what order
- Whether it runs on inputs the student never saw
- Whether they can explain and modify it live
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
"Build a tool that schedules the rigs" cannot be answered by a paragraph. The student has to make something real --- and defend it.
:::

## Grade the Process, Not Just the Artifact

::: {.three-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Runs on held-out data]{.card-title}

Test the deliverable on inputs the student never saw --- a fresh dataset, a new edge case
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Live modification]{.card-title}

"Add this feature now." Whoever built it can; whoever pasted it cannot
:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[Version history]{.card-title}

Git shows the build as a sequence of decisions, not a single drop
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The finance course this material grew from grades six group software deliverables plus peer assessment --- each one runs, and each one is defended.
:::

## Checking AI {.section-divider}

## Write vs. Critique

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Write the recommendation]{.card-title}

- Student makes the call --- finds the risks, proposes a fix, defends the tradeoffs
- The classic writeup
- In the open lane, AI helped draft it
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Critique the AI's recommendation]{.card-title}

- Student is handed a fluent, confident, subtly wrong AI memo
- Their job is to evaluate it, not write their own
- Tests whether they can judge AI output --- [the real skill now]{.accent}
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
Critique turns the course's own lesson on the student: they spend the term learning to distrust a confident AI, then are handed one to catch or approve.
:::

## Case Exams with AI, In the Room

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[The format]{.card-title}

- In class, no devices --- a genuine secure assessment
- Students are given an AI-generated solution to a problem
- They critique it: what is right, what is wrong, what is missing
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Why it holds up]{.card-title}

- You cannot outsource the judgment to the tool you are judging
- Tests the skill that matters when AI drafts everything first
- Open, AI-rich work outside; secure evaluation inside
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
The exam and the tutorbot are the same philosophy from opposite ends: let AI carry the content, and put the human's judgment at the center of what we assess.
:::

## Not Detection {.section-divider}

## Why Detectors Are the Wrong Tool

::: {.two-cards}
::: {.card .card-red}
[What fails]{.card-title}

- AI detectors are unreliable and produce false positives
- They are biased against non-native English writers
- Vanderbilt and others turned them off
:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[What works instead]{.card-title}

- State per assignment what AI use is allowed --- and why
- Design assignments AI cannot simply do, like critiquing an AI's answer
- Move the graded moment into the secure lane
:::
:::

::: {.explainer}
You will not win by policing the open lane. You win by designing assessments whose answer is judgment, and holding the high-stakes ones where you can see the student think.
:::

## Redesign, Don't Bolt On

::: {.three-cards}
::: {.card .card-blue}
[Weave it through]{.card-title}

IESE wove AI across 18 first-year courses --- not bolted onto a couple of electives
:::
::: {.card .card-amber}
[Rethink the core]{.card-title}

If AI does the analysis, what should the analytics course now assess? The applied skill, not the mechanics
:::
::: {.card .card-teal}
[Move up the ladder]{.card-title}

Free graded time from content and mechanics for framing, judgment, and defense
:::
:::

## The Through-Line {.centered-statement}

::: {.card .card-dark}
AI now does the middle --- the drafting, the coding, the analysis. So assessment moves to the ends: [deciding what should be done]{.accent} and [judging whether it was done well.]{.accent} Flip the room, assign things that run, and make students check the AI. That is what we are here to measure.
:::

## Breakout {.section-divider}

## Questions to Discuss

- Which of your current assessments is a take-home that AI can now do end to end?
- Where is your secure lane --- and is the high-stakes grade actually held there?
- What would a "build something that runs" deliverable look like in your course?
- Would you rather have students write the recommendation or critique an AI's? Why?
